extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mass communication / media studies; instructors and researchers interested in external influences on news content
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter excerpt that catalogs and explains external forces shaping mass-media content (governmental censorship and policy, regulation, military constraints, marketplace competition, ownership, and community relations). Useful for analyzing how non-media organizations affect news production and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government censorship powers and bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments can ban broadcasts or publications and revoke credentials when content is deemed dangerous or to incite violence (examples: UK ban on broadcasts by Irish organizations; Israel shutting down Palestinian media; credential revocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes overt actions (bans, shutdowns, revocation of press credentials) and legal/regulatory orders; examples show both wartime and peacetime uses. Anti-pattern: treating government statements about security as only rhetorical—these actions have tangible effects on who can appear and what can be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification requirements for journalists (mobility restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies can require specific qualifications for foreign journalists to work in another country (example: 1988 US-Canada provision requiring a college degree and three years' experience for Canadian journalists in the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such credential rules function as barriers to entry and can limit cross-border reporting and exchange of viewpoints; presented as a threat to freedom of expression when used to restrict journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: State ownership and direct control of media
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the state owns or controls newspapers, television, and radio (example: People's Republic of China), media content is directly shaped by ruling parties or government agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control mechanisms include ownership, licensing limits on new publications, appointment/management influence (journalists as civil servants), and unwritten rules about positive portrayal. Outcome: self-limiting reporting, rise of nonpolitical/entertainment content to maintain revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship induced by intimidation and arrests
rubrics_metrics.description: Threats, arrests, or other intimidations of journalists (example: arrests of Hong Kong journalists) lead to increased self-censorship and avoidance of politically sensitive topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without explicit legal bans, fear of reprisals alters editorial choices; manifests as underreporting or softened criticism of authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment vs. broadcasting licensing/public interest standard
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. First Amendment protections for print press are broad, but broadcast media must obtain licenses and are expected to 'serve the public interest'—creating a different legal/regulatory relationship with government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes laissez-faire treatment of print from regulated broadcast domain; operational consequence: broadcasters face more government pressure because of licensing and perceived duties to the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness Doctrine requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fairness Doctrine required broadcasters to provide time for opposing views and to act as 'fiduciaries' of the public trust (FCC policy adopted in 1949).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes its effect—intended to protect public interest but argued to have chilled speech—and subsequent policy changes (repeal) that altered broadcaster behavior. Scoring note: compliance shaped programming decisions and avoidance of controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of deregulation (including Fairness Doctrine repeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deregulation in the 1980s (repeal of Fairness Doctrine and other controls) changed content indirectly: reduced mandated accountability, fewer public-service obligations, and new commercial incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences listed: decline or removal of local news programming, rise of tabloid TV, greater commercial exploitation of children's programming, and overall shifts toward profit-driven content. Examples and studies cited to illustrate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-trafficking rule and license-holding requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The no-trafficking rule required broadcast licensees to hold licenses for at least three years; repeal made broadcast properties more liquid and increased short-term sales of stations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: frequent ownership turnover may reduce commitment to public-service programming. Note: the 1992 Cable Act retained an anti-trafficking provision for cable system owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public television editorializing rights
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1984 public television stations were given the right to editorialize, although this reportedly had little effect on content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible reasons for limited impact include journalistic timorousness; presence of rights doesn't guarantee practice change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of Information (FoI) presumption and classification review
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations (Society for Professional Journalists) and administration policies urged a presumption of public access, allowing secrecy only when disclosure would cause 'specific, identifiable harm'; executive actions periodically reexamine classification rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides journalists' expectations and administrative practice regarding access to government information; anti-pattern: blanket secrecy or long-standing habits among officials resisting FoI reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government information/propaganda apparatus (public information specialists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government agencies employ information specialists (over 3,000 U.S. workers noted) whose role is to ensure public media carry the 'desired message forward'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes techniques like leaks, backgrounders, and off-the-record briefings used to set the news agenda. Analysts should watch for agenda-setting via managed information releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive appeals for voluntary restraint in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Political leaders sometimes urge voluntary journalistic restraint in the 'national interest' (example: Kennedy's request during Vietnam buildup), attempting to influence news judgment without formal censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such appeals can create pressure to weigh 'Is it in the national interest?' alongside 'Is it news?' and may be met with resistance from publishers valuing editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence-agency relationships with journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported secret or cooperative relationships between journalists and intelligence agencies (e.g., CIA) can lead to insertion of material into media, provision of cover for agents, and influence over foreign-coverage content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranges from occasional favors to paid relationships; anti-pattern: undisclosed ties that compromise journalistic independence and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-policy influence on editorial stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Media coverage can follow shifts in government policy (example: US coverage of China shifted when government favored better U.S.-China relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies cited show correlation between policy orientation and press preference; suggests monitoring for policy-driven framing or selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic/visa controls as de facto censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Government decisions to deny visas or entry to foreign leaders or speakers (example: refusal to admit Castro and Ortega) can limit who addresses U.S. press forums and thus shape information available to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though justified on diplomatic grounds, such controls affect the range of viewpoints in public media events and conferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military-imposed reporting constraints in wartime (pooling, censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: During military operations, reporters may be subject to strict access rules: signing agreements, pre-clearance of content, embedding in military 'pools', restricted movement, and use of only approved pool footage (examples: Persian Gulf War restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects include heavy reliance on pool material, editing of reporters' copy for 'security', exclusion of independent reporters, and constrained framing of events. Anticipate language shifts ('neutralized' etc.) introduced by military phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOD National Media Pool membership criteria (proposed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed DoD criteria for inclusion in the National Media Pool: maintain a regular military correspondent; visit military units and attend Pentagon briefings; maintain sufficiently sized Washington bureau; be ready to deploy within four hours with equipment; agree to ground rules and mission-specific rules; be U.S.-owned and operated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit checklist shaping who gains privileged access; acceptance implies agreeing to operational constraints and could bias pool coverage toward outlets meeting DOD's familiarity and readiness standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and language control by military and officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials and military actors establish preferred language/frames for events (e.g., 'knocked down', 'neutralized', 'taken out') that soften perceptions of destruction and shape reportage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists may adopt 'soft words' that obfuscate violence; analysts should flag euphemistic language as a sign of agenda or framing influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate ownership and conflict-of-interest effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate ownership ties (example: GE owning NBC and supplying military equipment) can create conflicts where journalists praise equipment or policy that benefit parent corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for favorable coverage of corporate or commercial interests tied to owners, sponsorships, or advertisers; such ties can bias story selection and evaluative language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketplace competition assumption about diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevailing assumption is that competition among media creates diversity (a 'marketplace of ideas'), but empirical studies show mixed results—often little difference in editorial content between competing newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume competition automatically increases diversity; research evidence cited both supports and challenges the hypothesis depending on medium and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive positioning among TV stations
rubrics_metrics.description: Television stations attempt to position newscasts differently to attract audiences, producing unique local stories; competition can therefore create diversity in local news coverage (Atwater findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local broadcast diversity may arise from strategic differentiation; local market structure and station strategies matter when assessing variety of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution concentration and cable content homogenization
rubrics_metrics.description: Expansion of cable and many channels has not necessarily increased content diversity because much programming comes from a few distribution companies and consists of reruns or familiar formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should consider supply-chain concentration (few distributors) and programming reuse when evaluating claims of greater diversity due to more channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/community characteristics shaping content
rubrics_metrics.description: Community attributes (size, economy, culture, spatial layout) affect media content: larger markets produce more spontaneous-event coverage; smaller markets rely on preplanned features, wire copy, and serve booster roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: larger stations/newspapers run more original/exposé material; smaller outlets lean on wire services and community boosterism. Consider budget/staff constraints as mediating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic conditions affecting newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: National or industry economic changes influence perceived newsworthiness (example: network coverage of the oil industry increases as oil prices rise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News attention can track economic salience rather than intrinsic news value; use circulation or market metrics to predict coverage intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community relations and publisher boosterism
rubrics_metrics.description: Local publishers may act as 'community boosters'—promoting economic development, supporting local campaigns (e.g., saving military bases), and shaping placement and tone of stories to help the community's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boosterism can alter editorial priorities (front-page placement for favorable stories, burying unfavorable ones) and conflict with independent reporting; note instances where editorial departments are pressured to support the owner's profit goals.
